summary: For 6–8 year-olds learning to identify and name local plants and animals, including microhabitats (under a log, in a pond, in leaf litter). The core work is first-hand observational fieldwork: search real tiny places, identify and name what lives there using a simple picture key, and link each creature to the microhabitat's conditions (damp/dark suits woodlice). The central insight is that different tiny places shelter different, suited creatures — grounded in observation, not recall of exotic species. A searchable scene can scaffold the nested-scale idea, but because the curriculum prioritises first-hand fieldwork it supplements rather than replaces a real minibeast hunt.
misconceptions: Naming only exotic animals (lions, tigers) rather than the organisms actually present locally.
Not recognising a microhabitat as a habitat — thinking 'under a log' is too small to count.
Assuming the same creatures live everywhere, missing that conditions sort them into different microhabitats.
Overlooking plants and tiny invertebrates as part of the habitat's life.
Thinking a creature is 'lost' rather than suited when found in a damp/dark place.

activities.title: Real minibeast hunt: search, name, and record conditions
steps: Go outdoors to a local habitat (garden, school grounds, park) and gently search several microhabitats: lift a log, turn a stone, dip a net in a pond, part the long grass, sift leaf litter.
For each find, use a simple picture key / spotter sheet to identify and say the creature's NAME aloud (woodlouse, centipede, pond skater, tadpole, grasshopper, worm).
Attach a conditions tag to each microhabitat: damp, dark, wet, sunny, dry — and say it ('under the log is damp and dark').
Keep a tally/species list of what lives where, then compare: which microhabitat had the most living things?
Model respectful practice throughout: look closely, record, and return every creature and replace each log/stone where it was found.
activities.insight: Different tiny places (microhabitats) within one habitat have different conditions, and creatures are usually found where the conditions suit them; a microhabitat is a small habitat inside a larger one.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: where will more minibeasts live?
steps: Before looking, predict: 'Will I find more minibeasts under this damp log, or on this sunny open patch / brick wall?' and state WHY.
Lift the log (or paving slab) and check the sunny patch; observe what is actually there.

Compare the prediction with what you actually found and explain it: for example, if you found woodlice or worms under the damp log but not on the sunny wall, why might that be? If your results were different, talk about what might explain that.
Transfer the reasoning to a new place: name two creatures that live in the pond water (such as tadpoles or pond skaters) that you would not expect to find under a dry log, and say why.
activities.insight: Creatures are not scattered at random; they are mostly found where the conditions (damp/dark vs hot/dry) suit what their bodies can tolerate — a woodlouse left in the hot sun soon dries out.

activities.title: 'Microhabitat' means a small place, not a small animal
steps: Point to the log and say what bigger habitat it is part of (the whole garden/wood).
Explain in your own words that a microhabitat is a small habitat INSIDE a larger one.
Find a creature that is bigger than you'd expect in a tiny place (e.g. a centipede under a small log) to show 'micro' is about the place, not the animal's size.
Give an example of a microhabitat and describe its conditions.
activities.insight: 'Micro' refers to the small scale of the place, not the size of the animals that live there; a small habitat still counts as a habitat.

activities.title: Searchable habitat scene (scaffold for the nested-scale idea)
steps: In a local-habitat scene, search by tapping to lift a log, dip a net in the pond, or part the long grass; each search reveals the creatures that live there.
Read the name label and conditions tag (damp, dark, wet, sunny) that pops up for each find, and say the name aloud.
Watch a species list / tally build as you search, then compare which microhabitat held the most creatures.
Use matching and picture-identification activities ('which lives under a damp log?') to check naming and link each organism to the microhabitat whose conditions suit it.
activities.insight: Reveal-on-search gives immediate naming feedback and shows that different tiny places hide different suited creatures; it rehearses the nested-scale idea when outdoor fieldwork is not available.

checkQuestion: Tell the child: 'Under a damp log I found woodlice and worms. On a sunny brick wall nearby I found none of them — but I did see a butterfly.' Ask: 'Why do the woodlice live under the log and not on the sunny wall? What is it like in each place?'
checkAnswer: Under the log it is damp and dark, which woodlice need — they dry out and die in the sun. The sunny wall is hot and dry, which suits sun-loving insects but not woodlice. Different microhabitats have different conditions, and each creature is found where the conditions suit it.
